children: Preferred shares issued by major U.S. banks such as Bank of America Corp. and Wells Fargo & Co. differ sharply from their common stock. They typically carry a fixed dividend that must be paid before any common dividend, rank senior in the capital structure during liquidation, and generally confer no voting rights.

Because most bank preferreds are perpetual and trade like long-duration bonds, their market prices are highly sensitive to interest-rate expectations rather than the banks' earnings growth. Consequently, the recent behavior of these securities provides an important indication of the rate outlook.

The lack of a meaningful rally in bank preferreds suggests investors are not yet pricing in a sustained decline in interest rates. In other words, the preferred market continues to lean toward a "higher-for-longer" rate regime, with expectations for meaningful cuts in the near term remaining subdued.
Here's a look at the weakness in Bank of America and Wells Fargo preferreds, along with the stubbornly high 10-year Treasury yield, now near 4.8%.

A look at Bank of America Series QQ this year shows that the softness began with the bearish death cross in March. Notice the gap down on May 1, followed by a bullish inverse head-and-shoulders formation that took shape through May and June. The brief breakout above the pattern and the 50-day simple moving average failed in late June, leading to a bear flag formation.

A bullish morning star completed on August 18, indicating selling pressure was abating. However, Friday's break below the $16 pivot shifts the setup back to the bearish side. The shares could move lower toward $14.75 in the near term, representing an 8% decline from current prices.

The Wells Fargo Series CC shares show a similar picture. Weakness accelerated in late February with bearish shooting star candles on February 18 and 19, followed by doji candles in four of the next five sessions. That marked the beginning of a long bearish descending triangle with a decisive break below the $17 trigger in late July serving as an ominous sign. Early and late August brought retests of the breakdown, but both failed at the downward-sloping 50-day SMA, confirming the break lower.

A bullish morning star completed on August 19 but failed to generate any meaningful upside progress. More recently, a bullish piercing line candle formed on September 2, on one of the strongest volume days of the year, yet it also failed to produce any follow-through to the upside. The inability of either bullish signal to spark a sustained recovery reinforces the bearish tone of the setup.

Meanwhile, the technical picture for the CBOE Treasury Note 10 Year Yield shows a bullish slant over the past year. It repeatedly found support at the "round" 4% level, with bullish engulfing candles on September 17 and November 18, 2025, three dojis in the second half of October, and a bullish morning star on March 2. These signals repeatedly marked periods when buyers stepped in at or near the 4% level.

A bullish golden cross in late March kicked off a cup with handle that broke out on May 13, followed by a double bottom on July 13 and a bull flag above a 4.75% pivot on August 31. The succession of bullish patterns points to continued upside in the yield. The technical setup points to a move toward 5.1% by year-end.

Regardless of the asset class, trends are more likely to remain in motion than to reverse. That makes the persistent weakness across bank preferred shares a sign that interest rates could remain elevated for some time. If weakness were isolated to just one or two securities, it could be easily dismissed as company-specific. Instead, weakness across the majority of major bank preferreds suggests the pressure is broader and that investors continue to demand higher yields. In turn, that points to interest rates remaining elevated, with the risk of further increases still intact.
